power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A number of other studies have focused on the clinical significance of TMBs on MRI specifically in mTBI patients (GCS 13-15). Although there has been some evidence of an association between TMBs on MRI and higher symptom severity at 1 year in mTBI, 11, 13 most studies have not demonstrated an association. Einarsen et al. 9 found no statistically significant association of TMBs with postconcussive symptoms in mTBI in 183 patients at 3 months or in 167 patients at 1 year. Similarly, Huovinen et al. 12 studied 113 mTBI patients with MRI at 3-17 days post-injury, and found no difference in GOSE or return-to-work at 3 months. Van der Horn et al. 6 showed that TMBs, while common even in CT-negative mTBI (referred to as "uncomplicated" mTBI 29 in that study), had no association with outcome in 54 CT-negative patients, even at 2 weeks post-injury. Although the results presented here may appear to conflict with these studies, a reasonable explanation is that the prior studies did not have sufficient power to detect a significant association with GOSE at p<0.05. Einarsen et al. 9 performed power calculations that suggested at least 300 or more mTBI patients would have been required to demonstrate a statistically significant effect at p<0.05, based on the prevalence of postconcussive symptoms in their study sample. This greatly exceeds the numbers of patients evaluated in any of these studies. Furthermore, the mTBI patients in Huovinen et al. 12 sustained significantly milder injuries than the TRACK-TBI mTBI subgroup: 56% attained a GOSE score of 8 by 3 months post-injury, compared to only 40% in TRACK-TBI; and only 34% of mTBI patients had any traumatic intracranial findings on brain MRI, compared to 43% in TRACK-TBI patients with GCS 13-15.

Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "A number of other studies have focused on the clinical significance of TMBs on MRI specifically in mTBI patients (GCS 13-15). Although there has been some evidence of an association between TMBs on MRI and higher symptom severity at 1 year in mTBI, 11, 13 most studies have not demonstrated an association. Einarsen et al. 9 found no statistically significant association of TMBs with postconcussive symptoms in mTBI in 183 patients at 3 months or in 167 patients at 1 year. Similarly, Huovinen et al. 12 studied 113 mTBI patients with MRI at 3-17 days post-injury, and found no difference in GOSE or return-to-work at 3 months. Van der Horn et al. 6 showed that TMBs, while common even in CT-negative mTBI (referred to as \"uncomplicated\" mTBI 29 in that study), had no association with outcome in 54 CT-negative patients, even at 2 weeks post-injury. Although the results presented here may appear to conflict with these studies, a reasonable explanation is that the prior studies did not have sufficient power to detect a significant association with GOSE at p<0.05. Einarsen et al. 9 performed power calculations that suggested at least 300 or more mTBI patients would have been required to demonstrate a statistically significant effect at p<0.05, based on the prevalence of postconcussive symptoms in their study sample. This greatly exceeds the numbers of patients evaluated in any of these studies. Furthermore, the mTBI patients in Huovinen et al. 12 sustained significantly milder injuries than the TRACK-TBI mTBI subgroup: 56% attained a GOSE score of 8 by 3 months post-injury, compared to only 40% in TRACK-TBI; and only 34% of mTBI patients had any traumatic intracranial findings on brain MRI, compared to 43% in TRACK-TBI patients with GCS 13-15."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p<0.05", "p<0.05", "p>0.05", "p<0.05", 
"p<0.05"), Text = c("Although imaging features associated with intracranial mass effect fell short of statistical significance except at the 2-week time point, this is likely due to the relatively low prevalence of these imaging features and GOSE-TBI scores <5 in the GCS 13-15 subgroup, rather than decreased importance: the odds ratios for these features, though not significant at p<0.05, are relatively large.", 
"Large markers (triangle, square, or circle) are used to emphasize o statistically significant odds ratios (p<0.05) from Tables 2 and 3.", 
"Small markers (also triangle, square, or circ denote odds ratios from Tables 2 and 3 with p>0.05.", 
"Although the results presented here may appear to conflict with these studies, a reasonable explanation is that the prior studies did not have sufficient power to detect a significant association with GOSE at p<0.05.", 
"Einarsen et al. 9 performed power calculations that suggested at least 300 or more mTBI patients would have been required to demonstrate a statistically significant effect at p<0.05, based on the prevalence of postconcussive symptoms in their study sample."
)), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p>0.05", Sentence = "Small markers (also triangle, square, or circ denote odds ratios from Tables 2 and 3 with p>0.05."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::
